name: mpack
workload: Encode (write), tree-parse and incremental-parse of randomly generated schemaless objects (2367-byte 'small' and 248571-byte 'large' MessagePack documents with mixed maps, arrays, strings, ints, doubles), hash time subtracted.
claimed_speedup: Write, small: MPack 2.13 us vs msgpack C 6.42 us and msgpack C++ 2.77 us. Write, large: 307.27 us vs 544.24 us (C) and 347.14 us (C++). Tree parse, small: MPack 4.99 us vs msgpack C 6.47 us and msgpack C++ 9.40 us. Tree parse, large: 414.16 us vs 750.87 us (C) and 1004.67 us (C++). Derived from page data: encode 3.0x (small) and 1.8x (large) over msgpack C, 1.3x and 1.1x over msgpack C++; tree parse 1.3x and 1.8x over msgpack C, 1.9x and 2.4x over msgpack C++. README: 'MPack outperforms all JSON and MessagePack libraries (except CWPack), and in some tests MPack is several times faster than RapidJSON'.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.3.0 on Arch Linux; -Wall -O3 -flto -fno-fat-lto-objects -DPIC -fPIC -DNDEBUG (-O3 and -flto always enforced)
hardware: AMD Phenom(tm) II X6 1090T (x86_64, 6402 bogomips) desktop PC; also a first-generation Raspberry Pi table
tradeoffs: C library, amalgamation (mpack.h and mpack.c) embeddable, runs on 8-bit microcontrollers and in the Linux kernel; MessagePack only (not a JSON drop-in); stateful error handling instead of per-call return codes; tree API gives an immutable node tree; README recommends the Expect API (known schema) for maximum performance, which that suite does not cover.
caveats: Benchmark is written and run by the MPack author (the suite's own disclaimer says it may be biased). Benchmarked MPack is 0.8.1 and msgpack-c 1.3.0 (2016-era, GCC 5.3.0, Phenom II) while the README now describes MPack 1.1 and msgpack-c 3.3.0, so current ratios are unknown. Tree-parse and incremental rows are not all wins: libbson's tree row is faster (4.45 us small, 301.90 us large) and libbson is BSON not MessagePack. The README claim 'except CWPack' is not backed by the suite README, which lists CMP, msgpack and MPack as MessagePack implementations but not CWPack. msgpack C encode row (6.42 us) is the weakest baseline; msgpack C++ is only 1.1x to 1.3x behind on writes. Ratios are derived from the page tables.

name: mrpt-serialization
workload: Serialize and deserialize a gtsam::Values plus gtsam::NonlinearFactorGraph (Pose/Point/Rot values, Prior and Between factors with noise models) through mrpt::serialization archives versus GTSAM's Boost binary archive, graph sizes N = 1, 5, 25, 100, 500, 2000, results on a log time axis.
claimed_speedup: README of MRPT/gtsam2mrpt_serial: 'approximately 2x faster serialization and deserialization for mid-sized factor graphs' and 'roughly half the wall-clock time of GTSAM's native Boost binary serialization'. Exact timings exist only in two PNG plots (docs/profiling-ser.png, docs/profiling-deser.png), not in text.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700HQ @ 2.60 GHz, Ubuntu 20.04, Boost 1.71, MRPT 2.4.4
stars_or_usage: 2.2k stars (mrpt/mrpt); 7 stars (gtsam2mrpt_serial); packaged for ROS 2 Humble to Rolling
tradeoffs: mrpt-serialization is a versioned, endian- and word-size-stable binary archive (mrpt::serialization::CArchive) driven by CSerializable class registration and stream operators, with optional gzip or zstd streams via mrpt-io; it is not schema-based like protobuf, and the faster path in the benchmark needs the gtsam2mrpt_serial bridge library plus MRPT 3.x.
caveats: The benchmark is in a separate repo (MRPT/gtsam2mrpt_serial, same organisation, so first-party) and measures a GTSAM bridge built on mrpt-serialization, not the core library on generic data. Baseline is Boost.Serialization through GTSAM, not protobuf, FlatBuffers or another widely known serializer; no direct protobuf comparison was found. Compiler and build flags are not stated, the README numbers come from MRPT 2.4.4 on Ubuntu 20.04 (the repo now requires MRPT 3.0), and the exact timings are only in log-scale images, so only the rounded '2x' claim is quotable. The profiling code (tests/main.cpp) is public and only compiled when GTSAM uses Boost, and it uses mrpt::system::CTimeLogger with max(5, 1000/N) repetitions.

name: musl
workload: 32 libc micro-benchmarks (ns per operation) built with zig cc for x86_64-linux-gnu and x86_64-linux-musl: e.g. atoi over 512 short decimal strings, strtok and strtok_r CSV splitting, bsearch on ints, strrchr, sprintf('%.6f') over 128 doubles.
claimed_speedup: musl vs glibc ns/op (third-party table, mixed result): atoi_parse 3.96 vs 9.28; strtok_r_parse 4.94 vs 14.76; strtok_parse 5.71 vs 15.23; strrchr 157.31 vs 354.19; bsearch_int 10.52 vs 16.02; sprintf_float 136.34 vs 160.56. Derived from page data: 2.3x, 3.0x, 2.7x, 2.3x, 1.5x and 1.2x faster. glibc is faster in 20 of the 32 rows (e.g. qsort_int 2.8x, strtod 4.3x, strstr 2.9x, malloc_free_small 11x, strncmp 37x), 3 rows tie.
compiler_and_flags: zig 0.15.2 (clang 20.1.2) 'zig cc' with -std=c11 -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto=full -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops -DNDEBUG -fno-math-errno -fno-trapping-math -g0 -s, targets x86_64-linux-gnu and x86_64-linux-musl (run.sh)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U, Linux 6.8.0-87-generic (Ubuntu 22.04), run dated 2025-11-18
stars_or_usage: 400 stars (kraj/musl, a downstream mirror of the official musl git); benchmark repo 7 stars
tradeoffs: Repo description stresses efficient static and dynamic linking, lightweight code and low runtime overhead rather than peak throughput. In the same table musl's malloc (malloc_free_small 11x, malloc_free_medium 4x slower), qsort (2.8x), strtod (4.3x) and several str* routines (strcpy 5.9x, strncmp 37x slower) lose badly to glibc; musl+jemalloc closes most of the malloc gap. Software relying on glibc-specific behaviour may need porting.
caveats: Weak claim: musl wins only 9 of 32 rows against glibc and loses 20; a faster-than-glibc statement holds only for the rows named. The benchmark is a one-person third-party repo (fereidani/musl-vs-glibc, 7 stars, no licence on the repo page) and is not like for like: the glibc binary comes from zig cc's glibc stubs and the system glibc at run time (dynamic) while musl is linked statically, and -flto=full lets the compiler inline statically linked musl code. The 16 KiB memcpy row (glibc 4043.27 ns vs musl 154.19 ns, 26x) is implausible for a real glibc and should be treated as an artifact. The musl project's own home page, wiki and git host and the etalabs libc comparison were unreachable (egress blocked), so any project-side startup-time or size claims could not be checked. The record is filed under the 'musl' project because the repo itself carries no benchmark.

name: mmx sdefl/sinfl (single-header deflate)
workload: Deflate compression and inflate decompression of a roughly 100,000,000-byte text corpus (ratio column implies 100 MB, probably enwik8; the header does not name it), compared at several compression levels.
claimed_speedup: Table in sdefl.h and sinfl.h. Compression: sdefl -0 127 MB/s vs zlib -1 72 MB/s; sdefl -5 45 MB/s vs zlib -6 24 MB/s; sdefl -7 38 MB/s vs zlib -9 20 MB/s. Decompression: sdefl 355 to 436 MB/s vs zlib 307 to 314 MB/s. Compressed ratio about equal (sdefl -5 36.46 vs zlib -6 36.55). Derived from page data: compression 1.8x, 1.9x and 1.9x over zlib at comparable levels; decompression 1.2x to 1.4x. vs miniz 1.0 -1: 127 vs 122 MB/s compress, 355 vs 208 MB/s decompress.
tradeoffs: Small ANSI C (C89) single-header deflate (525 lines) and inflate (320 to 500 lines), about 3.7 KB each as WebAssembly; API is one-shot buffers (sdeflate/zsdeflate, sinflate/zsinflate) for raw deflate and zlib framing, with no gzip container or streaming interface found; the repo's other headers (json.h, sched.h, web.h) carry no performance claims.
caveats: First-party table in the header comment with no CPU, compiler, flags or corpus name, and no benchmark code in the repo; library versions (zlib 1.2.11, libdeflate 1.3, miniz 1.0) place it around 2020 to 2021. The same table shows libdeflate 1.3 clearly ahead of sdefl (147 MB/s compress at -1, 667 to 689 MB/s decompress), so sdefl is 'faster than zlib' but not the fastest deflate. Listed repo vurtun/mmx has been renamed vurtun/lib (the Readme title still says mmx). The comparison picks the sdefl and sinfl components out of a five-header collection. No independent measurements were found. Ratios are derived from the page table.

name: netbsd-curses
workload: Build and install of the library, programs, shared and static libs and headers (make -j2 all install) on a dual-core x86_64 sabotage Linux system with built-in terminfo and widechar support.
claimed_speedup: README Table 1: build time (make -j2) 59 sec for ncurses vs 9 sec for netbsd curses (6.6x, derived from page data); installed size 15.9 MB vs 1.3 MB; size of libncursesw.so 346 KB vs 150 KB; extracted source 15.8 MB vs 3.3 MB; static-linked nano 334 KB vs 288 KB.
compiler_and_flags: CFLAGS '-g0 -fdata-sections -ffunction-sections -Os -fno-unwind-tables -fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables -Wa,--noexecstack', LDFLAGS '-s -Wl,--gc-sections -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now' (README Appendix A); compiler not named
hardware: dual-core x86_64 sabotage Linux system (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Close to a drop-in ncurses replacement with widechar support, but no mouse handling (no-op macros), only 510 color pairs, missing rarely used functions such as vidputs(), different struct layout (some programs such as Python's curses module need patches), curses and terminfo are split into libcurses and libterminfo, and terminfo is a CDB database.
caveats: The claim is build time and footprint, not runtime curses performance; no runtime benchmark against ncurses was found. Single run, no repeats or variance, ncurses and netbsd-curses versions not stated, and the configure-heavy ncurses build is single-threaded for part of its time (the README says netbsd curses should scale better with more jobs, which is untested). Binary size table is a size-optimised (-Os) build. First-party numbers, no benchmark script in the repo.
